title: Behind the Monastery
text:
Behind the monastery, beside the road,

there is a cemetery of worn-out things,

where rusty iron lies, pieces

of crockery, broken pipes, twisted wires,

empty cigarette packs, sawdust

and zinc, aged plastic, broken tires,

waiting like us for the resurrection.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the discard pile as a cemetery of objects waiting for resurrection.

title: Epigram
text:
In losing you, you and I have lost:
        I, because you were what I loved most,
        and you, because I was the one who loved you most.


        But of the two of us, you lose more than I do:
        because I will be able to love others as I loved you,
        but you will not be loved as I loved you.
editorial_note: This source preserves the indented epigram form while matching the already translated argument about unequal loss.

title: Corn Island
text:
The water of South

West Bay is bluer

than the sky


but your eyes are

bluer than

South West Bay


And in the caves of

(...)

May rains

have already arrived,


the red malinches

have bloomed again


And the road to

Diriá is cheerful

full of puddles;


but you are no longer

with me
editorial_note: The translation preserves the Caribbean place names, the ellipsis, and the final absence after the rains return.

title: I Who Have Had the Bad Luck
text:
I who have had the bad luck

that God fell in love with me.

I have been left out of the erotic game.

Others in those games will laugh at me.

When my love in Granada

was unlimited, were you jealous?

My sexual desires have been and are

only analogies of my love for you.

I think my sexual desires please you.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the poem's frank erotic theology and its address to God as beloved.

title: Song
text:
My long hair!

My long hair!


You wanted your

girl with

long hair


I have it below

my shoulders


Do you think this corner

of the guava seller


where you found me

with terror and with joy


(although you only showed

paleness and silence)


will be erased by

Los Angeles,

les Champs—Elysees?
editorial_note: The translation keeps the remembered street corner against glamorous later geographies.
